> I'm making this custom macropad, and it's built to control my workflow. Specifically, it will feature six tactile buttons mapped out for frequently used hotkeys, two rotary encoders that let me dial in step-by-step changes, and an onboard OLED display that dynamically shows system stats right on the device, and may do other fun things with it. (stay tuned!) Code will be written during build week!

## Design

### 2026-10-11: The first hour consisted of nothing much but research into parts and fitting within the budget. I ended up settling on these parts, as seen in the image below.

**7h**

The first hour consisted of nothing much but research into parts and fitting within the budget. I ended up settling on these parts, as seen in the image below.

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 150711](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/2921df7d1438104c107f809aab1037e5a335e1c69833e30819b1505ec5ea0e74.png)

Hours 2-7 all consisted of working inside KiCad to build and test the PCB.

For the PCB layout file, I built out a standard 1.6 mm thick board on an A4 sheet using KiCad. On the board, I used a USB-C connector for power and data, the RP2040-Zero as the computer, a couple of rotary encoders for dial controls, six tactile switches for the macro buttons, and an OLED display for visuals. To wrap up the power side, I added a 3.3V regulator along with its supporting components.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/6f6c4dfe9877947a67334e78a8016a9e2e59694b699146eea5d5d6ef5e32cd97.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/93a04b6a166d99aa3f422c3f152267bc2e179c4ca4b10abdc4310f4e8baa8d09.png)

 I set standard DRC rules in the project config file. Tracking a minimum of 0.2 mm, zero clearance, and 0.5 mm spacing from the board edge, while the default net class runs 0.2 mm tracks, 0.2 mm clearance, and uses 0.3 mm drill / 0.6 mm outer diameter vias to tie everything smoothly over to the main schematic file.

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 160624](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/4c7cdf34164fe4e972d7a2daa708bbf860bafa7a202dcf0d747f8744ce3f6a61.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 160720](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/2cc6d7211c2b3fea3882ae8ba731cb5db89edd55aa4cb6c8a5f48306939f7ee6.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 160901](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/1dfe3e6964fd4cb2ba128cb11ae9a6c754b691c5bd50ee433e9e26a79b25ed38.png)

For the schematic, I split the layout into neat, manageable blocks covering USB power and regulation, the RP2040 controller, custom buttons, rotary dials, and a status display. Finally, I wired up all the key nets, including VBUS, +3V3, GND, the button lines, the encoder pins, ENC1_PUSH, and the I2C bus lines.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/ae1d1c89df665b954f870a3923c5b0633365344cbadc82800cf47d374276b1a0.png)

## Build

### 2026-11-14: In the first hour, I soldered the OLED's and RP2040 Zero's pins to each other, respectively, and started to plug a few of the parts together on the breadboard because measure twice, cut once, right...

**7h**

In the first hour, I soldered the OLED's and RP2040 Zero's pins to each other, respectively, and started to plug a few of the parts together on the breadboard because measure twice, cut once, right....?(Foreshadowing)

![20261114_223921 1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/ac01512b62ac28dda5485d93db12cad7ef2c9392853175e49ce3c6234d3f7747.jpg)

From the middle of the second hour to the end of the third, the TL,DR version is: I had a lot of trouble getting the parts to respond and communicate.

I first had to go online and figure out how to install an IDE to get started with pushing over code. I then installed the appropriate libraries that I would need to start coding (Thanks, Adafruit!!! Love you guys; thanks for putting them all together no hunting required. Very helpful). At first, I struggled and tried to use the Arduino IDE (thinking because they are more reputable it should be ok) but it was not. Then I stumbled upon an Adafruit guide (which uses a macro pad kit called the 5100 that also uses the RP2040 Zero) that recommended the "Mu Editor", which made life so much simpler when editing and for pushing the code later.

Until a few minutes later, when my RP stopped showing up as a drive that I could dump files and edit the code. It took about two hours to troubleshoot and fix because there were so many possibilities regarding the issue (Was it my computer's hardware or software, was it the parts that I bought? Was it just a setting in my computer or how about a missing driver?). The final solution that worked consisted of me getting a tool called Zadig to reinstall the drivers on the RP2040 Zero, going into the Device Manager and doing some investigating there.

![Screenshot 2026-11-14 215744](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/bfc2b5aa843c532405b1b7e296a27eda079d05f049a106bc3ea2f25bb14a9a64.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/fpT4vKaaCxCaCu9yi3OynxGXkAPlXNzI/c86d06112e345a05af59cbcd3dbea2a598083749bfb338c88b06f01d21ee4f12.png)

The next 3 productive hours included finishing some preliminary coding to make sure my wiring was actually correct and also mainly to see if the parts work because I was interrupted the first time.  The nice part about the Mu editor is that it is in Python, which is a much simpler language to read and code for beginners like myself. The code is below, and I put in comments for each step on what they do for each part.
